variants.headline: Our new vassalage under {{master}}
body: Our nation now answers to {{master}} as a vassal. A clerk in the chancery has tied the two treaty copies with one cord. When their court calls, our towns must answer.

variants.headline: An era of our own counsel, concluded
body: Here closes the chapter in which our {{terms.civic.government}} gave its orders and no other court confirmed them. In this year we became vassals to {{master}}. The scribe has ruled a line beneath the entry, so a reader may see where our own counsel ended.

variants.headline: Tell us what protection we bought
body: Vassals to {{master}}! That is the word on every step this morning, and no one has told us what it costs. The {{terms.civic.government}} must read the terms aloud in the square. If our sons can be marched to their wars, we should hear what their court promised in return.

variants.headline: Our neighbors have a new court to bargain with
body: Neighbors with a dispute against us now have a second court to persuade. Our vassalage to {{master}} puts a foreign government between their complaint and our answer. Whether that makes them bolder depends on how the {{player.civic.government}} of {{master}} reads its obligations.

variants.headline: Our defensive pact with {{ally}} is over
body: The foreign office has marked the end of our defensive pact with {{ally}}. The two countries remain at peace, so no soldier is called anywhere today. The promise that each would answer for the other is simply gone.

variants.headline: A defensive pact comes to an end
body: One of our defensive pacts has lapsed. The two countries remain at peace, and neither owes the other troops.

variants.headline: An attack on {{ally}} is their problem now
body: The end of the pact with {{ally}} leaves our generals with one fewer certainty. A campaign that once promised a second army now promises only our own. Planners who counted on borrowed strength must find something else to count, or ask for less.

variants.headline: Will you still send the next load?
body: Sir, the end of the pact with {{ally}} was read at the exchange, and a friend who keeps a warehouse across that border asked whether I would still send my goods. I told him I would. His clerks have never lost a crate of mine, and I will not insult them over a change in the courts.

variants.headline: We sign a defensive pact with {{ally}}
body: A defensive pact with {{ally}} is signed and sealed. In the square, the crier had the news before the clerks had filed it. The meaning is plain: a blow at either country brings both to the field.

variants.headline: A defensive pact is signed
body: Our nation has signed a defensive pact with a major power. The terms bind each signatory to answer an attack on the other. No names are needed to make that promise heavy.

variants.headline: Hear it! We stand with {{ally}}
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! The pact with {{ally}} is signed, and the seal is dry. Raise a hand against them and you raise it against us. Say that at every door: one blow, two answers!

variants.headline: A pact for the {{terms.civic.government}}, a question for the street
body: Our {{terms.civic.government}} has tied its word to {{ally}}'s safety. That may be statecraft, or it may be a bill sent to our sons. Let the terms be read aloud where the recruits can hear them, and let the men who must march know what for.

variants.headline: Letters from the {{terms.civic.government}}: a pact with {{ally}}
body: We are informed by letters from the {{terms.civic.government}} that a defensive pact has been concluded with {{ally}}. Such an agreement asks little of either people in quiet seasons. It asks much of both on the day a neighbor forgets his manners.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} denounces our nation
body: {{civilization}} has denounced our nation before the world. A doorkeeper read the declaration from the steps of the foreign ministry, and the crowd carried it home in pieces. No treaty is torn up today, but the courtesy is.

variants.headline: The square heard it first
body: By noon the whole market knew: {{civilization}} has denounced us. A fruit seller says she had it from a sailor, who had it from a clerk, who had read it twice. By closing time the tale had grown a battle, a rescue, and a hero on a white horse.

variants.headline: Let the denunciation be answered
body: {{civilization}} has spoken against us in open court. Let their ministers shout until they are hoarse; our business is the frontier and the muster roll. A soft answer to a loud insult is heard as fear, and fear is remembered.

variants.headline: In this year, {{civilization}} spoke against us
body: In this year {{player.leader}}, {{player.civic.leaderTitle}} of {{civilization}}, delivered a denunciation of our nation before witnesses. The scribe has copied the words beside the date. The margin is left empty for what follows.

variants.headline: First contact with {{stranger}}
body: Envoys have returned with the first confirmed meeting between our nation and {{stranger}}. Each side now knows the other's name and face. The age of guessing is over.

variants.headline: They say strangers came over the hill
body: They say a hunting party found tracks by the spring that no one could name, and followed them two ridges over. At the top they met {{stranger}}, and shared a fire without a word in common. The hunters came home late, and their story has been walking since.

variants.headline: A new people, and new roads to walk
body: Advices from the frontier report that envoys from our nation and {{stranger}} have met and spoken. The meeting was formal, cautious, and long enough to leave a written account. Both courts can now write to each other by name.

variants.headline: We just met {{stranger}}
body: We have met {{stranger}}. One more people beyond the hills, one fewer mystery. More when the envoys report.

variants.headline: The mapmaker has a question about {{stranger}}
body: Sir, since word of {{stranger}} arrived, my customers have asked for charts of country I have not walked. I will not ink a line I cannot stand behind. Send me the survey notes from that meeting, and the next map will be honest, even if it is plain.

variants.headline: {{first}} and {{second}} sign a defensive pact
body: Word reached the harbor at noon: {{first}} and {{second}} have signed a defensive pact. A broker read the notice twice before he would price the news. A quarrel with one of them now carries a second name.

variants.headline: Two foreign powers bind their defenses
body: Two foreign powers have signed a defensive pact. Neither signature is ours, but both now count in our own plans. Any quarrel with one of them must expect the other.

variants.headline: The pact between {{first}} and {{second}} redraws the arithmetic
body: The pact between {{first}} and {{second}} changes the arithmetic in every staff room. A plan against either country must now leave room for the other's banners. That may make neighbors careful, or it may gather several quarrels into one. The first true test will come at a border, not at a signing.

variants.headline: From abroad: {{first}} and {{second}} stand together
body: Letters from abroad relate that {{first}} and {{second}} have signed a defensive pact. A cloth merchant in our own market, who buys from both countries, has begun splitting his orders between them. If trouble starts at one frontier, he does not want his whole season waiting there.

variants.headline: {{first}} and {{second}} end their defensive pact
body: {{first}} and {{second}} have ended their defensive pact. The notice came through the foreign office with no ceremony and no explanation. Neither country has promised troops to the other since.

variants.headline: A foreign pact falls away
body: Two foreign powers have dissolved a defensive pact between them. Neither has taken up arms against the other, and no third party was asked to witness the parting.

variants.headline: The quiet between {{first}} and {{second}}
body: The pact between {{first}} and {{second}} has been dissolved. Their neighbors once weighed a quarrel with one and counted the other's army in the answer. Now an envoy must judge each court on its own temper, with nothing on paper to bind the two replies.

variants.headline: The fence between two gardens
body: Two gardens shared one fence, and one morning the posts were gone. The beans still climb, and the rabbits have learned the way.

variants.headline: We declare friendship with {{friend}}
body: Our nation and {{friend}} have declared friendship. At the granary, a clerk pinned the notice beside the price of salt. The goodwill is now public, and merchants on both sides can plan as if it will last.

variants.headline: A friendship declared
body: Our nation has declared friendship with a major power. Both governments have said so openly, and each has promised the other fair dealing. The promise is easy today; the years will show what it is worth.

variants.headline: Hear it! Friendship with {{friend}}
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! {{friend}} is a friend of this nation, and the declaration is signed. Friendship with {{friend}}, open and sworn! Say it at the well, say it at the gate, and say it again for the people at the back!

variants.headline: Sir, a good word travels slowly
body: Sir, I drive a wagon between your country and {{friend}}'s, and the news of the friendship reached me late, at the last inn on the road. The drivers I meet are quicker to share a fire and slower to quarrel. I hope the two courts keep it so, because my family eats from that road.

variants.headline: The tavern drank to {{friend}} last night
body: When the crier called the news, the tavern keeper set a jug on the bar and named the first cup for {{friend}}. Nobody asked him to. He says a friendly road brings carts, carts bring thirsty drivers, and that is reason enough.

variants.headline: Our friendship with {{friend}} is over
body: The declaration of friendship with {{friend}} has been withdrawn. At the wool exchange, a broker has stopped quoting their houses in the same breath as ours. The two countries still trade, but the warmth is gone from it.

variants.headline: A friendship ends
body: A declaration of friendship with a major power has lapsed. The two governments still keep the peace, but the public pledge of goodwill no longer stands between them.

variants.headline: In memoriam: the friendship with {{friend}}
body: For a few seasons it was the sort of friendship that gets its own toast at public dinners. The declaration is ended now, and the toasts have gone quiet. What the two peoples keep is a habit of courtesy that may yet outlast the paper.

variants.headline: The end of the {{friend}} friendship, weighed
body: The friendship with {{friend}} has ended, and the record now says less than it did last season. A declaration of this kind lends no troops, but it lends confidence, and confidence is what merchants price into a road. The first sign of the change will be quieter correspondence, not louder threats.

variants.headline: Our court takes {{vassal}} as a vassal
body: {{vassal}} has become a vassal of our {{terms.civic.government}}. At the palace, a clerk has added their name to the list of courts that answer to ours. The tribute will be counted later; the obligation begins today.

variants.headline: {{vassal}} entered in the roll of vassals
body: In this season the envoys of {{vassal}} came before our court, and their nation became our vassal. Their {{player.civic.government}} keeps its hall and its officers. The first tribute is due at the turn of the year, and the scribe has made a column for it.

variants.headline: A new source of tribute, a new frontier to defend
body: {{vassal}} now pays tribute to our court, and the money will be welcome. So will the duty of defending them, which no one has yet priced. A vassal is a promise of help, and the promise is only as good as the road our soldiers can march.

variants.headline: Let the magistrates of {{vassal}} set out what they can pay
body: The {{terms.civic.government}} has won the right to set a tribute on {{vassal}}. A generous figure would please the square and ruin the collection. The proper course is to ask the provincial officers what the land yields, then take a little less. A tax that breaks the payer is a tax paid once.

variants.headline: {{vassal}} is no longer our vassal
body: Our court no longer holds {{vassal}} as a vassal. The tribute office has struck their name from the roll, and a clerk has filed the old accounts. From now on, the two courts deal as equals, or not at all.

variants.headline: One vassalage ends
body: A vassalage that bound another state to our nation has been dissolved. The tribute stops, and the obligation to protect them stops with it. The two governments now meet as separate courts.

variants.headline: {{vassal}} walks free of us
body: {{vassal}} has left our protection, and the frontier feels the difference first. A garrison captain who once counted their militia in his plans must now write them out. Every other court that pays us tribute will be watching to see what we do about it.

variants.headline: The vassalage of {{vassal}} comes to an end
body: The vassalage of {{vassal}} has ended after a term that neither court now cares to celebrate. The clerks who once copied their accounts into our books have been reassigned. What remains is a treaty in a drawer and a road that no longer carries orders.

variants.headline: We and {{civilization}} denounce each other
body: {{civilization}} and our {{terms.civic.government}} have denounced each other in the same season. Both declarations are public, and neither court has left itself a quiet way to withdraw. A broker at the exchange read both notices, then quietly raised what he charges to carry goods on that road.

variants.headline: Both courts put their quarrel on record
body: Both our court and {{civilization}} have put a denunciation on paper. Their envoys may still meet behind a door, but each side has said in public what it cannot easily take back. From here, every small quarrel has a written precedent.

variants.headline: Two houses, one quarrel
body: Two neighbors shout across the wall. The mason sells them both a higher wall.

variants.headline: Who pays for the shouting?
body: Our {{terms.civic.government}} and {{civilization}} have traded denunciations, and the bill will be paid in some street. A printer on the wharf has already been asked to set the notice twice, once for each side. Ask the government plainly which of our livelihoods it is willing to spend on this quarrel.

variants.headline: We open our borders to {{civilization}}
body: Travelers from {{civilization}} may now cross our frontier without stopping for a permit. The order went out to every post this morning, and the first carts were through before noon. Our borders are open to them, and the toll houses will have the paperwork to prove it.

variants.headline: Our borders stand open to a neighbor
body: Our nation has opened its land to a neighboring power. Their carts and their travelers may cross as they please, and no frontier post will ask for a fresh permit. The roads will be busier, and the garrisons will have more faces to watch.

variants.headline: Notice to merchants: our roads are open to {{civilization}}
body: Notice to merchants: the frontier is open to {{civilization}} as of this morning. Their caravans may pass without a fresh permit, and their traders may deal where they like. Toll clerks have been told to expect a busy road.

variants.headline: Open borders with {{civilization}}, and the goodwill they carry
body: Opening the border to {{civilization}} puts their carts on our roads and their money in our markets. It also gives their court something to lose if the frontier turns ugly. A crossing that carries goods both ways is worth more than the soldiers who used to watch it.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} opens its borders to us
body: The frontier posts of {{civilization}} have been ordered to let our people through. A courier tested the order yesterday and crossed without showing a paper. Their land is open to us now, and our caravans may follow at will.

variants.headline: A neighbor opens its borders to us
body: A neighboring power has opened its roads to us. Our traders may cross their land without a permit for every trip, and our couriers need not wait at the post. The welcome is new, and it is worth using before it cools.

variants.headline: The road to {{capital}} is open
body: The road to {{capital}} is open, since {{civilization}} has lifted its frontier permit for our caravans. A carter who has spent years quoting that route at a cautious price is now promising a faster one. His customers are listening.

variants.headline: One wagon, loaded by noon
body: The carter at the north gate had his wagon loaded by noon, and not with market goods. He heard that {{civilization}} had opened its border and packed for a look at the other side. "All my life I have hauled along that fence," he says. "Now I want to see what is behind it."

variants.headline: {{from}} and {{to}} bargain, and a war ends
body: {{from}} and {{to}} have struck a bargain, and part of the price is peace with a third state. In the border town, a shopkeeper has begun taking the boards from her windows. She has heard promises before, but this one came with signatures.

variants.headline: Peace is part of the price
body: A bargain between two states has been entered in the record, and it buys quiet on a third frontier. One of the signers has promised to end a war with a state that had no seat at the table. The state that was fighting has not been heard from yet.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && fromGives !== null && toGives !== null
variants.headline: The terms, as recorded
body: {{from}} puts in: {{fromGives}}.
{{to}} puts in: {{toGives}}.
The entry that matters: a war closed by signature, not by a battle.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && ours === false
variants.headline: A war ends at someone else's table
body: The deal between {{from}} and {{to}} carries peace to a third state that had no seat at the table. Officers there will hear it from a courier, long after the ink dried. Such arrangements end a war quickly and leave the men who fought it asking what was promised over their heads.

variants.headline: War is written into the deal between {{from}} and {{to}}
body: {{from}} and {{to}} have agreed on a deal, and war against a third state is part of the price. A courier stopped at the posting house for a fresh horse and would not say where he was bound. The stable boy noticed the direction and kept it to himself.

variants.headline: A deal with war in the terms
body: A bargain between two states has been entered in the record, and one clause is a war. The signer has promised to take up arms against a country that had no voice in the deal. That country will learn of it from an envoy, or from the first horseman.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && ours === false
variants.headline: Tonight: a deal that buys a war
body: Tonight, {{from}} and {{to}} have signed a deal, and the price includes a war. The third country named in the terms has made no answer. We are watching the border and will bring you word as it comes.

variants.when: from !== null && to !== null && ours === false
variants.headline: Other people's wars, other people's coin
body: The deal between {{from}} and {{to}} spends a third nation's peace without asking its leave. Our government was not at the table and has said nothing since. It should tell the country now whether our trade roads will be guarded, and by whom.

variants.headline: Our vassalage to {{master}} is over
body: The vassalage to {{master}} has ended, and the tribute rolls have been closed. Our {{terms.civic.government}} speaks for the nation again without another court's leave. The first test will come the next time a neighbor asks who speaks for us.

variants.headline: We are no longer a vassal
body: The vassalage that bound our nation to a foreign power has ended. No tribute leaves our treasury for another court, and no foreign envoy signs our orders. The government answers to its own people again.

variants.headline: Hear it! We bow no more
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! {{master}} holds no claim on us this morning. The vassalage is ended, and our {{terms.civic.government}} gives its own orders again. Shout it at the gate and shout it in the square: no master, no tribute, no bowed head!

variants.headline: In this year, the vassalage was dissolved
body: In this year our nation ceased to be a vassal of {{master}}. The scribe records the closing of the tribute rolls and the return of our seal. What the court does with that seal is not yet written.

variants.headline: Free, and with work to do
body: {{terms.civic.people}}, the oath to {{master}} is ended, and good riddance. Our {{terms.civic.government}} should now show that it can stand without a patron. Let every envoy's instructions be read aloud before he leaves, so we know what is said in our name.

variants.headline: We denounce {{civilization}}
body: Our {{terms.civic.government}} has denounced {{civilization}} in public. The declaration is copied into the day book, and other courts may now read exactly where we stand. The words will outlast the anger that produced them.

variants.headline: Said plainly, and none too soon
body: The denunciation of {{civilization}} is signed, and it was a long time coming. A denunciation will not stop a single company of spears. It does tell every court in the world which way we will face when the trumpets sound, and that is worth the paper.

variants.byline: A reader who trades across that border
variants.headline: Sir, was there no quieter road?
body: Sir, I read that our {{terms.civic.government}} has denounced {{civilization}}, and I think of the wagons that cross that border every week in both directions. A quarrel is easy to announce and hard to feed. If the words can be softened without shame, I would ask the government to soften them.

variants.headline: In this year, we spoke against {{civilization}}
body: In this year the {{terms.civic.government}} spoke against {{civilization}} in the hearing of other courts. The scribe has written the words exactly as they were delivered. No comment is added here, and none is needed yet.
